name: Motivated B-Roll Story Sequence
source_tutorial: knowledge/research/transcripts/what not to do in editing.txt
use_when: A documentary or vlog section has abundant B-roll but weak story motivation.
Shots are being inserted only to cover dialogue or avoid talking-head duration.
Narration or interview lines mention places, stakes, scale, details, or consequences that can be visualized.
A slide, screenshot, proof frame, or B-roll shot can show exactly what the speaker is referencing.
A simple short-form talking-head edit needs a few B-roll shots placed on key lines.
B-roll text sequences can show an experience, emotion, or contrast while text names the beat.
avoid_when: The B-roll is intentionally abstract or atmospheric and the user wants ambiguity.
The shot would imply something untrue or unsupported.
The visual is attractive but unrelated to the current beat.

timeline_pattern.wide_close_rule: Use wide-to-close pairs when the story needs epic scale and human detail.
timeline_pattern.pattern_rule: Set up, confirm, and reaffirm visual patterns unless breaking the pattern is a deliberate comedy or surprise beat.
timeline_pattern.map_rule: Hold maps and route graphics until the stated distance or destination is understandable.
timeline_pattern.spoken_reference_rule: When the speaker names an object, person, result, UI, or proof point, the supporting visual should appear close enough to that line to feel motivated.
timeline_pattern.broll_text_rule: When text sits over B-roll, choose the shot for the story beat first, then add readability treatment only as needed.
timeline_pattern.short_form_amount_rule: For simple short-form edits, gather roughly 3-4 usable B-roll shots and place them where the message changes or needs proof.

motion.rule: Use one strong establishing/drone shot plus one or two smooth focal-point shots rather than many quick, weak shots. For B-roll text sequences, darken or desaturate footage only enough for the overlay text to read.
motion.avoid: Rapid B-roll strings with no scan time or focal point.

sound.rule: If one B-roll shot has sync sound, build a consistent ambience rule for the sequence.
sound.short_form_rule: Mute or delete B-roll source audio when it competes with talking-head A-roll.
sound.avoid: Silent filler B-roll beside isolated random sync sounds.

captions.rule: Captions should support the story beat and not replace the need for motivated visuals.

color.rule: Match B-roll color enough that the sequence feels intentional, especially when mixing stock and original footage.

implementation.ffmpeg: Use contact sheets to identify repeated shots and weak focal points. Build EDL rows with beat labels and visual motivation notes.
implementation.remotion: Represent B-roll beats as data with fields for narration cue, visual evidence, duration, ambience, and focal point.
implementation.blender: Use map or scale graphics only when they clarify geography or contrast.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Replace filler B-roll with shots that directly answer the current line; hold map/route graphics long enough to read.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Create bins for scale, detail, normal life, danger, testimony, and contrast; assemble by beat rather than source order. Use Source Monitor I/O points, drag video-only when needed, and place readability adjustment layers between text and B-roll.

common_mistakes: Cutting B-roll just because the talking head has been on screen too long.
Repeating the same shot because the edit schedule is rushed.
Using wide-to-wide-to-wide when the viewer needs human detail.
Showing a map or route too briefly for the viewer to understand it.
Using B-roll only to avoid a talking head while the visual does not match the spoken idea.
Leaving B-roll source audio under the speaker by accident.
Darkening or desaturating B-roll so much that the viewer loses the proof or action.
qc: Can every B-roll shot be tied to a story point?
Are repeated shots intentional and rare?
Does the sequence include both scale and detail when needed?
Can the viewer understand maps, routes, and graphics before they disappear?
Does the sequence avoid filler shots with unclear focal points?
Does each visual arrive close enough to the spoken reference it supports?
Is unwanted B-roll source audio removed or intentionally mixed?
If text is over B-roll, does the readability treatment preserve the story detail underneath?
